data.description: Establish a standard way to discuss what Kjerneverk is and create standards for generating text about the project

data.content:
What's driving the need for messaging standards? Am I finding inconsistencies in how a journey of work is described across different packages? Difficulty explaining the project. I'm finding that every time I ask cursor or a model to generate copy for a website or to describe the thing, we don't really have one document that describes what is Kjerneverk.

I want to do that right now. So, Kjerneverk is a way for us to make sense of using LLMs to execute certain things. Prompts are really a form of execution, right? When we create a prompt, the idea behind Riot Prompt originally was just create a way to standardize the format of prompts. Create a way to track the structure of a prompt. You can do it in code, you can put it in a file format. Prompts right now are really this freeform block of text. But in reality, as we start to use these tools more, prompts have sections. And the initial model for prompts is extensible, but you've got a persona, we've got instructions, you've got context. And Riot Prompt was really designed for the initial phases of generative AI, like back when we were just sending prompts over to conversational tools and getting one response.

But, Riot Prompt has been extended to now support agentic interactions. And it's great. But the purpose of Riot Prompt is to assist people that need to create prompts, that need to store them somewhere, that need to load them somewhere, that need to exchange them. Ultimately, the long-term roadmap for Riot Prompt is that it's a library that you use to get your prompts ready to send to whatever model you're using. I actually do think that one of the original reasons for it is still valid. Back when we were creating these million token prompts and that was the thing that we thought we were going to be doing, one of the ideas in Riot Prompt was to be able to put a bunch of context in it and then cull the prompt using some sort of numeric prioritization. We're not really doing that now because we've moved over to agentic and Riot Prompt has expanded to support agentic work. Plus, Riot Prompt also has expanded to start supporting the execution of the prompt itself. Originally we didn't do this, but we definitely have gotten to that point.

So when we're describing what Kjerneverk is, we need to take some of the ideas that I just talked about with Riot Prompt into effect. And what I'll tell you right now is like when I am thinking about... I'm not thinking about AI development. That's what you put on the website for Kjerneverk is wrong.

Let's talk about Riot Plan. So, Riot Plan was sort of the next step. When we started to use generative AI and large language models, we would send it a prompt, we would craft the prompt to be perfect. We might do a follow-up prompt, but conversations were one or two or three things. It wasn't a real conversation and there wasn't this idea of MCP tools that the models have access to. What we're really doing is just saying like we're going to create a prompt, run it. But now that we have a more agentic approach, we can create plans.

But all the tools that came out with plans, they were just these really dumbed down plans. Like it was like a one or two pages and it was just like oh hey look you can do this you can do that and I had a different idea because I was doing really complicated things. I was trying to do migrations from one library to another or integrate a new library into a system. And I needed to create plans that did analysis, I needed to create plans for plans.

So I created RiotPlan and RiotPlan has developed into this tool that I use to really think about plans before we execute them. You can't just create a plan and just say, go do it. Yeah, great. Sometimes you need to create a plan and then you need to think about it and provide input and elaborate on an idea, explore an idea. Sometimes you need to do research to inform what a plan is. So that's what RiotPlan is. And RiotPlan is also gonna support creating a plan through MCP tools, which is what I'm doing right now. And Riot Plan itself is going to be the way that I do most of my work. I'm dictating a note to Riot Plan right now.

So that also needs to play into the description of what Kjerneverk is. And the last thing is Riot Doc. I write a lot of documents. I write a lot of blog posts. I write a lot of work documents, emails. I wanted to create a construct. I'm using the word construct on purpose because it's not a skill, it's not a format. I mean, it is kind of a format. Prompt, Plan and Doc are formats ultimately. But I built tools around the formats. And those tools and resources and prompts are there to help guide the models as they act upon those formats or as they use those formats to inform their execution.

And that really is kind of the core concept of Kjerneverk: I'm trying to define common formats, common approaches to things that we're doing using generative AI. The first and most generic is a prompt. Creating a prompt shouldn't just be like, "Here's a blank canvas. Type some text." The second is a plan. Same thing. You shouldn't just be like, oh, I'm going to create a plan. Let me just write a big multi-paragraph explanation of what I do. There's structure, there's status, there's infrastructure to support the execution of those plans. And documents. Documents, I've always wanted to be able to create a standard for documents that doesn't just store the output, that doesn't just store what you're writing. It stores the conversation towards the research, towards the evidence. And that's what I think Riot Doc is going to be. Riot Doc is going to be the way that I can have an idea, explore the idea, turn into an outline, turn into a draft, revise drafts, keep track of that process in a way that I think will support the document.

But this is what I'm saying, like, difficulty explaining the project to new users. I just talked for like 10 minutes. We can't put a 10 minute intro onto the website. But I would really love that Kjerneverk website to have a document that captures some of these ideas and puts it into like a one or two pager. I also do need, like, an elevator pitch. I need, like, a 30 second thing like, well, what is, what is Kjerneverk? I need an answer to that. And I also need something that like explains how the project works. Something like a glossary that defines some of the terms. I do need a document that has like tone and voice guidelines. What is the tone of Kjerneverk? What do we say? How do we say it? And it would be good to have target audience definitions as well.

So that's kind of what I'm saying. We need to create a communication standard for the document because it has to inform all of the properties that are describing what this thing does. And the reason why I think it's important is because I think more people are going to be paying attention to this thing going forward.

data.note: Core concept: Kjerneverk defines common formats and approaches for working with generative AI - Prompts, Plans, and Documents as structured 'constructs' with tools and infrastructure around them

RiotPrompt: Standardizes prompt structure (persona, instructions, context). Originally for single-shot prompts, now extended for agentic interactions and execution. Goal: library to prepare prompts for any model

RiotPlan: For complex, thoughtful planning beyond simple task lists. Supports analysis, elaboration, research, and thinking before execution. Designed for complicated work like migrations and integrations. Now supports MCP tools for plan creation
RiotDoc: Standard for documents that captures not just output but the conversation, research, and evidence. Supports idea → outline → draft → revision workflow with full process tracking
Key messaging problem: Every time AI generates copy about Kjerneverk, there's no single source of truth. Need one canonical document that captures the vision
Important distinction: This is NOT about 'AI development' - that framing is wrong. It's about structured formats and tools for working with generative AI
Needed deliverables: 1) 30-second elevator pitch, 2) 1-2 page overview document, 3) Glossary of terms, 4) Tone and voice guidelines, 5) Target audience definitions

data.constraint: Must avoid framing Kjerneverk as 'AI development tools' - that's not the right positioning
Needs to work for multiple audiences: users creating prompts/plans/docs, developers integrating the libraries, and AI assistants generating content
Must be concise enough for website use (can't be a 10-minute explanation) but comprehensive enough to capture the vision
Timing matters - more people will be paying attention to this going forward, so messaging needs to be ready

data.content:
About the construct concept: A prompt is bigger than just the text you end up sending to the LLM. It's the process you use to develop it. A prompt can have almost a superposition of states as well. Prompt evolves over time. A prompt could be the subject of experimentation. You could have revision one of a prompt, revision two. I think a prompt needs to have the ability to have more structure and meaning that's independent of any individual large language model you use it with. And that's why, if you want to think about RiotPrompt, it's a construct. It forms an object model, if you will, to think about prompts within. But it also forms a format.

Again, one of the initial reasons for this was OpenAI and Anthropic have different standards to delineate sections. If you have very large contexts like if you have a million tokens, you're supposed to use Markdown sections to delineate your sections on OpenAI and I think JSON or XML tags on another. And that was really the motivating factor on RiotPrompt. But then as we started to get into it, there are different large language models that have different standards for sections like Google that has a very rich collection of sections that you can send in your prompt that will control how the prompt behaves. I wanted something where you could write one prompt and then have it translate between the different large language models. So that's the construct.

Plans, the same thing. Everybody's coming up with plans to have their own formats, their own ways to do it. I wanted to just create one standard way, not just to store the plan, but a standard lifecycle to create the plan, a standard way to create a process. I'll use the word skill, but it's more a prompt in an MCP server - a prompt that knows how to access the resources that are in a plan through MCP and then invoke tools through MCP that direct a model to run it in the right way. So, in that sense, a prompt is bigger than just a prompt. A plan is bigger than just a plan.

And to bring it to sort of the thing that I think people are going to pay the most attention to: documents. What I want to capture with documents is when you read a good document, there's meaning in the document. But as an author, you spend so much time constructing that meaning from various sources and various references. And you can see some of that in a research paper in an academic setting. There are references and you can see it. In an academic research paper, you have to publish the recipe or the ingredients for how you came up with it.

But even when we're thinking about something that people might think is mundane, like a work email. When I'm writing a work email, I'm sending it to an audience. And there's a lot of science that goes into who is that audience? What are their motivations? What am I trying to achieve? And if we're going to use these large language models to really create things that we can call our own, I think the way we do that is by giving the user the ability to affect and manage complex context. I'll use the word ontology, although I worry about using that word too much. But if you think about ontology and the word construct, what I'm doing with documents, with prompts, and with plans is I'm trying to define that the thing is bigger than just the thing. It's a process. It's a lifecycle. It's a series of ways you access and think about it. It's a series of ways you come up with a plan or you come up with a document.

And that is the thing that I think is missing in word processors for documents or tools like Microsoft Project for plans. Something where you can really own it and drive it.

One other piece of feedback: I'm giving you a lot of really good content in this narrative. I would love for you to capture this because this is like a blog post. So in the plan somewhere, really capture this feedback that we need a couple of documents that really outline the deep philosophical meaning of Kjerneverk. And that's kind of what I'm getting at. When I see the website and what you put on the website, when I asked you to generate one, it was like, 'Kjerneverk is for AI development.' It's like, that's not what it's for. Kjerneverk is designed to help redefine how we think about prompts, how we think about plans, how we think about documents.

Target audience: Developers can integrate this library and use it. People creating prompts, plans, and docs - I'm hoping they can also use it from the command line, as an MCP or as an MCP server. I am actually going to try to ship some applications that people can download that'll make use of it. The primary audience are sort of technical users, technical people who are using generative AI who are sort of closer to programming than not.

My tone is pragmatic, it's opinionated, it's process focused. Another thing about my tone is that it's not willing to simplify things just to make it easy. I think that's one of the problems with large language models is that we're just throwing so much complexity at it, but we're afraid to use words like structure or ontology. I really think that one of the ways that we start appealing to people is by just being transparent that these are some really complicated concepts that we have to think about now. This is meta, metacognitive programming. There's a prompting approach called metacognitive prompting and that's prompting about prompting. Something I do a lot, even in these tools - ask the agentic workflow to do some self-reflection to give you some information that could affect the next invocation.

When we're writing a document, a lot of people will just fire up Word and start typing. Writers, good writers, will think about the process. I guess what I'm trying to get at is we'll all write better if we can think about the process, if we can really understand how it works. And I'm trying to create a process and a tool and standard that allows us to do that.

I don't know if I need an elevator pitch. I'm not trying to - this isn't the company. I'm just doing it because I want to. But let's see: Kjerneverk provides structured formats for some of the core ideas and concepts that you use when you're using generative AI, and tries to move away from freeform prompts and unstructured plans, or documents that are just generated from a model without your input, to giving you more control, giving you constructs, tools you can use to take back control over what you send to these models.

It's about control. But it's also an opportunity to really start to invest in how do we make sure that the prompts, the plans, and the documents that we're creating and getting from large language models are really our own and not just something that's copied from the patterns of the world. Large language models are really good at generating a document that just sort of hits the mark, but not quite. These tools that I'm creating allow you to really drive them towards what you want.

data.note: CORE INSIGHT: 'The thing is bigger than just the thing' - Prompts/Plans/Docs are not just artifacts, they are processes, lifecycles, and ways of thinking. This is the fundamental concept that must be communicated
Prompts have 'superposition of states' - they evolve, have revisions, are subjects of experimentation. Need structure and meaning independent of any specific LLM
Key differentiator: Write once, translate between LLMs (OpenAI uses Markdown sections, Anthropic uses XML tags, Google has rich section collection). RiotPrompt provides the abstraction layer
Plans are not just storage format - they include standard lifecycle for creation, standard process/prompts in MCP that know how to access plan resources and invoke tools correctly

Documents capture not just the output but the construction of meaning - sources, references, audience analysis, motivations. Like academic papers show the recipe/ingredients, all documents should track their creation process

Central thesis: To create things we can truly call our own with LLMs, we need the ability to affect and manage complex context/ontology. This is what's missing from Word processors and Microsoft Project

This is 'metacognitive programming' - prompting about prompting, self-reflection in agentic workflows. Not afraid to use complex terms like 'ontology' and 'structure' because these ARE complicated concepts
Key message: 'It's about control' - taking back control over what we send to models. LLMs generate documents that 'hit the mark, but not quite.' Kjerneverk lets you drive them towards what YOU want
Goal: Make outputs truly our own, not just copied from patterns of the world. Good writers think about process - these tools help everyone write/plan/prompt better by making the process explicit
CRITICAL DELIVERABLE: Need documents that outline the deep philosophical meaning of Kjerneverk. User's narratives are essentially blog post material that captures this philosophy
Target audience: Technical users closer to programming than not, using generative AI. Available as library, CLI, MCP server, and eventually standalone applications

Tone: Pragmatic, opinionated, process-focused, NOT willing to oversimplify. Transparent about complexity. This isn't a company - it's a passion project to redefine how we think about prompts, plans, and documents

data.constraint: Must NOT oversimplify - embrace complexity and use proper technical terms (ontology, structure, metacognitive). The audience can handle it
Must emphasize 'the thing is bigger than just the thing' - process, lifecycle, ways of thinking, not just artifacts
Core message must be about control and ownership - making LLM outputs truly yours, not just pattern-matched from training data

data.content:
Yes. Let's move on to shaping. And I'm going to give you some ideas before we get into it. First, I need those tone documents. I need the core message document. I need the target audience document. I'm not doing marketing here, but it would just be useful. I also need like a vision doc. Put those in the kjerneverk.github.io project, the website. That's a public project, but let's put it in there. Let's put those core sort of style guide, that sort of audience document, the tone, the voice, the core message. I want those to be like the sort of bible of generating content.

But then, I've given you a lot of narratives for each of the projects. If you look at the projects like RiotDoc, RiotPlan, RiotPrompt, all of those projects have a README file. They have a website. The README file is where you would expect it to be for the project. And the websites are in a docs subdirectory. What I would love for you to do for each of those websites is take some of the vision and some of the idea that I've talked about in this plan timeline. Take some of that vision and put it on those websites, put it in that README.

I'd also like you to maybe put a document together for the kjerneverk.github.io website. I'd like you to create a document that sort of - one for each of the projects like RiotPlan, RiotDoc, and RiotPrompt. And I'd love for you to talk about what they are in like a paragraph or two and then link to the website. I'd also love to have an overview page that takes some of the core concepts that I have talked about and put it on the website.

But really I think that's the shape. The shape is: Update the website, update the READMEs. Give me better language for those. Quick two or three sentence explanations. But then better language so that people that are showing up at these tools know what they're looking at. Right now, you show up at these websites, it's very confusing.

data.name: Comprehensive Documentation Update
data.description: Create foundational messaging documents in kjerneverk.github.io, then systematically update all project READMEs and documentation sites with consistent messaging
tradeoffs: Completeness vs Speed: Doing everything at once takes longer but ensures consistency
Centralized vs Distributed: Core docs in one place, but need to propagate to all projects

data.feedback:
Deliverables breakdown:

**Phase 1: Foundational Documents (kjerneverk.github.io)**
1. VISION.md - The philosophical foundation, 'the thing is bigger than just the thing'
2. CORE-MESSAGE.md - Control, ownership, structured formats for generative AI
3. TONE-VOICE.md - Pragmatic, opinionated, process-focused, not afraid of complexity
4. TARGET-AUDIENCE.md - Technical users working with generative AI
5. GLOSSARY.md - Key terms: construct, ontology, metacognitive programming, etc.

**Phase 2: Main Website (kjerneverk.github.io/public/README.md)**
1. Overview page with core concepts
2. Individual project pages (RiotPrompt, RiotPlan, RiotDoc) with 2-3 paragraph descriptions
3. Links to project websites

**Phase 3: Project-Specific Updates**
For each project (riotprompt, riotplan, riotdoc):
1. Update README.md with better language and 2-3 sentence explanations
2. Update docs website (docs/ subdirectory) with vision-aligned content
3. Ensure consistency with foundational documents

**Key Principle**: The foundational docs are the 'bible' - everything else derives from them

data.reason: This approach aligns with user's vision: create foundational 'bible' documents first, then systematically update all projects. Ensures consistency and provides single source of truth for content generation.

data.content:
For each of the projects, RiotPlan, RiotPrompt, RiotDoc, talk about a little bit of a before and after. Without RiotPlan, you're usually depending on the tools to come up with plans, and those plans are very inadequate. Some people have spent some time on planning - Beads is something from Steve Yegge, look that up before you write about it. But what I'm trying to do here is not just create another plan format, but a way for you to execute it that is - and again, this is one of the core concepts - independent of whatever tool you're going to ultimately use.

Call this out as one of the motivators for this project. We're too often getting distracted by the tools we use and not paying attention to the process. And as these models get better, it's starting to not matter which specific model you're using, or which tool you're using it in.

I've tried to design all of these tools so that they can be used by any model or no model at all. I mean, yes, some of the features we have are going to rely on thinking models. But I've tried to design RiotDoc, RiotPlan, and RiotPrompt so that you can use them from the command line and maybe throw it an OpenAI API key environment variable or an Anthropic Claude environment variable and make use of some of the agentic generation of content without having to do it from VS Code or your IDE. I think there's a lot of users out there who will do that.

I've also turned around and created MCP resources, tools, and prompts that'll work with each other and then literally use whatever model you've attached to that session. And then lastly, I am starting to think about ways to wrap these tools in more user-friendly ways like OS X apps.
